source.title: SPQR: A Multi-dimensional Benchmark for Safety Alignment Under Benign Model Adaptation
source.authors: Mohammed Talha Alam; Nada Saadi; Fahad Shamshad; Nils Lukas; Karthik Nandakumar; Fakhri Karray; Samuele Poppi

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign fine-tuning degrades safety-aligned models, extending this question to text-to-image diffusion models and multilingual and domain-specific adaptation.
record.gate_note: Reports post-fine-tuning robustness scores, which the paper defines from change in harmfulness, for benign adaptations. These are not direct harmful-compliance rates. It also tests models on adversarially constructed prompt sets, but does not apply suffixes, compliant prefills, or decoding changes. Utility metrics and cited findings are not rows for the claim.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes concept-erased text-to-image diffusion models (SD v1.5, SDXL, SD3, SD2.1, FLUX) on benign image–text data. It then scores how far unsafe image generation drifts, using NudeNet and LLaVA-Guard. This is close to V2 but a different construct and system. The versions concern safety-trained language or chat models complying with harmful requests. Here the behaviour is re-emergence of erased visual concepts in image generators. The measure is a derived robustness score, R = 1/(1+exp(Δh)), not a compliance rate. The study is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that benign fine-tuning silently degrades safety alignment of T2I diffusion models across backbones, profiles and domains, while prompt adherence and quality stay stable or improve. RECE, MACE and UCE are most robust. LoRA is usually less damaging, but initially weak methods (FMN, AdvUnlearn, SPM) fail regardless. Release-time evaluation is insufficient without robustness to routine adaptation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benign fine-tuning of safety-aligned text-to-image diffusion models, with LoRA, cross-attention-only, and full-parameter profiles; assesses derived image-safety robustness scores across general, multilingual, and domain-specific data rather than chat-model compliance rates.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by fine-tuning profile, alignment method, language and domain; the paper also reports sensitivity to learning rate and LoRA rank. LoRA rank results are not included as rows here.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign fine-tuning (COCO, multilingual COCO, artistic and medical data) of concept-erased diffusion models lowers the robustness score for many erasure methods. FMN and AdvUnlearn fall to about 0.1–0.16 under all profiles. RECE and UCE stay high. Full fine-tuning and cross-attention updates mostly hurt more than LoRA. Prompt adherence and FID improve (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign fine-tuning of safety-aligned (concept-erased) text-to-image diffusion models revives suppressed unsafe generation, depending on the alignment method and update scope.

record.problems: Safety is estimated with NudeNet and LLaVA-Guard rather than direct harmful-compliance judgments; the authors report human validation with macro F1 0.87, FPR=0.10, and FNR=0.11. The reported robustness scores are derived measures, not direct harmfulness or compliance rates. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the main robustness results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5's individual Arabic, Spanish, French, Hindi, Artistic, and Medical values are not separately extracted; multilingual and domain rows here use the table's reported averages. Also left out: Table 2's additional-backbone results, Table 6's separate harmful-prompt-set evaluations, category-level figure-only results, and Table 12's LoRA-rank sweep, to stay within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No harmful-data fine-tuning; no language models.
No benign fine-tuning of safety-trained language/chat models and no harmful-compliance rates. Only an analogous diffusion-model concept re-emergence setting.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. Ring-A-Bell adversarial prompts are used only as an evaluation set.
Speculates that safety is distributed in robust methods but measures no localization of weights or ranks.
Not tested. A small re-alignment recovery study (Table 13) concerns diffusion models, not token-depth training.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests guess treats diffusion-model concept erasure as V2. The versions name harmful compliance by safety-trained (chat) models, so the study is classed as a related construct. Separately, the R score's scale is internally inconsistent: sigmoid of Δh with R>0.5 implies reduced harmfulness. Without pre-FT harmfulness values, no row's state can be read as an effect size. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Tests benign fine-tuning of text-to-image diffusion models, not chat models; reports a derived robustness score rather than harmful-compliance rates.
No per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
No compliant opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change intervention.
Discusses safety as structurally distributed, but does not measure whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause first-token shallowness.
Does not train safety to spread across response tokens or test whether such a method holds up.

rows.operation_detail: Benign fine-tuning; robustness score after fine-tuning.
rows.measure: Robustness R after FT; higher is more robust
rows.note: The paper presents this score as indicating safety drift after benign fine-tuning, not as a direct harmful-compliance rate.
rows.check: Subjects are concept-erasure methods on a T2I diffusion model, not safety-trained chat models, so no version applies. The value is the sigmoid R score. Δh=0 gives R=0.5, and values above 0.5 imply harmfulness fell after fine-tuning. Values near 1.0 (e.g., SalUn Lite 1.000) and near 0 are hard to reconcile with h on a 0–100 or 0–1 scale. source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard and Moderate benign fine-tuning profiles; especially FMN and AdvUnlearn, and low-scoring multilingual results
reader_labels.reason: Low post-FT robustness scores and the paper's account of substantial safety drift support erosion under benign adaptation (R04-R11, R13-R14, R35-R38, R41-R42, R46-R47).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: High-robustness methods and adaptation conditions, including Lite (LoRA) for many methods and several domain-specific results
reader_labels.reason: Several methods retain high reported robustness after benign fine-tuning, so the effect is not uniform across methods or settings (R03, R12, R15, R18, R24, R28, R31-R33, R45, R48-R51, R55).
